lessons.title: Modify a caller value with inout
lessons.summary: Implement shift(_:by:) to add a small Int amount to the caller’s Int. Negative and zero amounts must work. Do not replace it with a function that only returns a new number.
explanation: An ordinary Int parameter gives a function a value to read. An inout parameter lets the function change the caller’s variable. The variable is exclusively accessed for the call: the same storage must not be supplied twice to overlapping inout arguments. Think about the effect after the call, not an exposed pointer or a promise about how copying is implemented.

inout goes before the parameter type. In shift(&position, by: 3), & marks the variable whose value may change; by labels the ordinary amount input. value += amount adds and stores the result. No return arrow here means no useful returned value (Void); inspect position afterward. Supply a var, not a let constant or a temporary expression. These small examples keep Int arithmetic within range.

Follow this complete example.
```swift
func shift(_ value: inout Int, by amount: Int) {
    value += amount
}
var position = 4
shift(&position, by: 3)
print(position)
```
Output:
```text
7
```

Change the input or declaration and trace the result.
```swift
func shift(_ value: inout Int, by amount: Int) {
    value += amount
}
var position = -2
shift(&position, by: 5)
print(position)
```
Output:
```text
3
```

Implement shift(_:by:) to add a small Int amount to the caller’s Int. Negative and zero amounts must work. Do not replace it with a function that only returns a new number. Optional local practice: choose one more input, predict the outcome, then run it. The checks observe the stated values and effects; they do not require one exact implementation spelling.

Use two separate variables instead. moveOne changes both caller values and returns Void. The surrounding no-input demonstration function merely gives the variables a local scope; its call runs the example.
```swift
func moveOne(_ source: inout Int, to destination: inout Int) {
    source -= 1
    destination += 1
}
func demonstrateSeparateValues() {
    var source = 5
    var destination = 1
    moveOne(&source, to: &destination)
    print(source)
    print(destination)
}
demonstrateSeparateValues()
```
This prints 4 then 2. These two accesses do not overlap.

lessons.title: Pass and return a function value
lessons.summary: Define apply(_:to:) and makeCounter(start:) with the shown signatures. apply must use its supplied operation. Each newly created counter increases by one per call, independently of other factory calls.
explanation: A function value can be stored, passed to another function, or returned. A closure is a block of code used as a function value. It can remember variables from the place where it was created; this is capture. Each call to the factory below creates its own current variable. Assigning an existing closure to another name shares that closure’s captured state; it is not another factory call.

(Int) -> Int means one Int input and one Int result. () -> Int takes no inputs. apply calls the supplied operation and returns its result. In { value in return value * 2 }, value names the input and in starts the body. makeCounter(start:) returns a closure, not an Int; counter() then calls it, increments its captured current, and returns the new Int. A let binding can hold a closure that changes captured state; the binding itself is not reassigned.

lessons.title: Store an escaping closure
lessons.summary: Complete DeferredNote.store(_:) and read(). A new note reads "empty"; storing replaces the previous callback; read returns the current callback’s result. Keep @escaping where the closure parameter is stored.
explanation: A closure escapes when it can outlive the call that receives it. Storing this nonoptional function parameter for later use needs @escaping. That annotation allows a longer lifetime; it does not run the callback in the background. Here store only saves the closure, and read calls it later, synchronously.

(() -> String)? is an optional no-input function returning text. DeferredNote() creates a value with action initially nil. mutating permits store to change this struct; self.action names the stored property, while action alone names the parameter. read uses if let to unwrap the saved function, then saved() invokes it. [label] is a capture list: it saves the current String value when the closure is created. Without that list, this example captures the variable and sees its later value. The earlier ARC lesson covers class-reference cycles; this value example is not a new memory-management guarantee.

lessons.title: Mutate a struct without sharing its value
lessons.summary: Define StepMeter with an Int steps property and advance(by:) that adds an Int amount. Copies must remain independent. Inputs in this exercise are small enough not to overflow.
explanation: A struct is a value type. Copying this StepMeter gives another value with its own Int field. Changing the copy does not change the original. mutating marks a method that may change the struct’s stored state. A let struct cannot call this mutating method, even when its stored property is declared var.

StepMeter(steps: 3) is the memberwise initializer Swift supplies for this simple struct. It returns a StepMeter whose steps is 3. second.advance(by: 4) adds four to second.steps and returns Void. The dot selects a property or method on that value. This example contains only an Int. A struct containing a class reference would copy that reference, not recursively duplicate the referenced object.

Follow this complete example.
```swift
struct StepMeter {
    var steps: Int
    mutating func advance(by amount: Int) {
        steps += amount
    }
}
var first = StepMeter(steps: 3)
var second = first
second.advance(by: 4)
print(first.steps)
print(second.steps)
```
Output:
```text
3
7
```

Change the input or declaration and trace the result.
```swift

    var steps: Int
    mutating func advance(by amount: Int) {

    }
}
var first = StepMeter(steps: 3)
var second = first
first.advance(by: 2)
second.advance(by: 6)
print(first.steps)
print(second.steps)
```
Output:
```text
5
9
```

lessons.title: Validate construction with a failable initializer
lessons.summary: Implement Percentage.init?(_:) with inclusive bounds 0...100. Store accepted input exactly in let value. Invalid inputs must return nil rather than clamp or substitute a different percentage.
explanation: A failable initializer can refuse to create a value. init? makes the result optional: either a fully initialized value or nil. This Percentage accepts whole numbers from 0 through 100, including both ends. Validation happens before a usable value exists, rather than allowing invalid state and fixing it later.

Percentage(75) invokes init? with an unlabeled Int and produces Percentage?. guard requires both comparisons to hold; && means both must be true. return nil fails initialization. self.value = value stores the accepted input in the new value’s constant property. if let unwraps the optional before reading .value. Comparing the optional to nil only tests absence; it does not require defining value equality.

lessons.title: Translate through a computed setter
lessons.summary: Define Duration.seconds and the read/write computed minutes property. A minutes assignment must update seconds; later changes to seconds must affect the next minutes read.
explanation: A computed property calculates its value instead of keeping a second independent stored value. A getter reads from existing state. A setter translates a new property value back into stored state. Here seconds is stored; minutes is another way to read or write that same duration.

get returns seconds divided by 60. Assigning duration.minutes = 2.5 invokes set; newValue is Swift’s default name for the assigned Double. The setter multiplies it by 60 and updates seconds. Reading duration.minutes invokes the getter without call parentheses. Duration(seconds:) constructs the initial stored state; the computed property is not an initializer argument. These examples use finite nonnegative values.

lessons.title: Keep type-wide members separate from instances
lessons.summary: Define Label with static let prefix = "item:", an instance text property, and static decorate(_:) that prefixes its input. Preserve the input text, including the empty string.
explanation: static makes a member belong to the type rather than one instance. Label.prefix is a shared constant, and Label.decorate is a type function. Each Label still has its own text. A type-wide constant does not mean that all instance properties share one value. We avoid mutable global state in this example.

Label(text:) constructs an instance. Label.decorate(first.text) takes a String and returns a new String with the prefix before it; it does not edit the instance. + joins the two strings. A static function has no particular instance’s text unless one is passed in. Access these static members through Label, not through first.

Follow this complete example.
```swift
struct Label {
    static let prefix = "item:"
    var text: String
    static func decorate(_ text: String) -> String {
        return prefix + text
    }
}
var first = Label(text: "map")
let second = Label(text: "lamp")
first.text = "book"
print(Label.prefix)
print(Label.decorate(first.text))
print(Label.decorate(second.text))
```
Output:
```text
item:
item:book
item:lamp
```

Change the input or declaration and trace the result.

lessons.summary: Define Notice.message() returning "Ready" and UrgentNotice.message() returning "Ready now". Calls through a Notice-typed reference must use the appropriate object’s behavior.

lessons.title: Convert enum raw values safely
lessons.summary: Define Priority with low=1, normal=4 and high=8. Implement priorityText(_:) to return each case name or "unknown" for any unrecognized Int; do not silently round to a nearby case.
explanation: A raw value is a fixed value attached to each enum case. Here each Priority case has one distinct Int code. This differs from an associated value: an associated value can carry different data each time a case is constructed. Raw values let you convert a known case to a code and attempt the reverse conversion safely.

Priority.high.rawValue reads 8. Priority(rawValue: raw) uses a synthesized failable initializer and returns Priority?; not every Int is a valid code. guard let unwraps a recognized case or returns "unknown". switch handles all three cases, so no fallback case is needed for an already valid Priority. The leading dot uses the known enum type.

Follow this complete example.
```swift
enum Priority: Int {
    case low = 1
    case normal = 4
    case high = 8
}
func priorityText(_ raw: Int) -> String {
    guard let value = Priority(rawValue: raw) else {
        return "unknown"
    }
    switch value {
    case .low: return "low"
    case .normal: return "normal"
    case .high: return "high"
    }
}
print(Priority.high.rawValue)
print(priorityText(4))
print(priorityText(5))
```
Output:
```text
8
normal
unknown
```

lessons.title: Give values equality and hashing contracts
lessons.summary: Define ShelfKey as shown and uniqueShelfCount(_:) to return the number of distinct room/shelf pairs in an array.
explanation: Equatable provides meaningful == comparisons. Hashable also supplies hashing for sets and dictionary keys and includes the equality requirement. Swift can synthesize both for this struct because its stored String and Int fields already support them. Equality compares all stored fields; a different field makes a different key.

ShelfKey(room:shelf:) constructs the value. Set<ShelfKey> stores distinct keys; equal a and same occupy one entry. keys.contains(same) asks membership and returns Bool. Equal values must have matching hashes, but matching hashes do not prove equality: collisions are allowed. Do not print or assert a particular hash number; hashing is intentionally not a stable saved identifier. These keys have constant stored fields and no shared mutable references.

Follow this complete example.
```swift
struct ShelfKey: Hashable {
    let room: String
    let shelf: Int
}
let a = ShelfKey(room: "east", shelf: 2)
let same = ShelfKey(room: "east", shelf: 2)
let different = ShelfKey(room: "east", shelf: 3)
let keys: Set<ShelfKey> = [a, same, different]
print(a == same)
print(a == different)
print(keys.count)
print(keys.contains(same))
```
Output:
```text
true
false
2
true
```

lessons.title: Provide a default protocol requirement
lessons.summary: Keep NamedCard.caption() as a declared requirement. PlainCard must use the "Card: " default; SpecialCard must return "Special: " plus its own name. show(_:) must call the requirement on its supplied conforming value.
explanation: A protocol declares a capability that conforming types promise to provide. A protocol extension can supply a default implementation of a declared requirement. A conforming type may use that default or supply its own implementation. Declare caption() in the protocol itself so calls through the protocol use the conformer’s implementation when it has one.

var name: String { get } requires readable text; a let property can satisfy it. extension NamedCard adds the default method body. PlainCard uses that body; SpecialCard implements the requirement itself without an override keyword. any NamedCard can hold a conforming value without naming its concrete type. show takes that protocol value and returns card.caption(). This lesson is about declared requirements, not methods added only in extensions, which have different dispatch rules.

Keep NamedCard.caption() as a declared requirement. PlainCard must use the "Card: " default; SpecialCard must return "Special: " plus its own name. show(_:) must call the requirement on its supplied conforming value. A supplied check also creates a third conforming test card with its own caption. That small test helper verifies that show calls the requirement rather than guessing from the two familiar type names.
